status_reason: The concept is blocked because a silica cable cannot carry mid-IR ATR, and the mid-IR fiber alternative depends on link length, routing and conditions that have not been supplied.
answer: The concept cannot be approved as stated: the visible/NIR silica cable transmits only to about 2400 nm, so it cannot carry MIR ATR spectra, and no mid-IR link reach for a remote analyzer is documented. Test MIR ATR for water in petroleum in the lab first, then screen CIR or PIR fiber once the link length and conditions are known.

inline.headline: Test MIR ATR for water in petroleum in the lab before approving any fiber link
inline.probe: ATR probe with a ZrO2 tip sealed in a PEEK shaft and protected by PEEK tubing
inline.install: in the petroleum line at the sampling point; location not yet supplied, with the analyzer remote
inline.fiber: mid-IR fiber (CIR 1.1–6.5 µm or PIR 3–17 µm), not the existing silica cable
inline.test_against: NIR transmission or transflection probe on the existing silica cable
inline.not_final_because: The water-in-oil example covers only 0.1–2.0% water with no detection limit, link length or process conditions, and mid-IR fiber reach is not documented.

problems.text: The existing visible/NIR silica cable cannot carry MIR ATR: silica transmits about 350–2400 nm, while the water-in-oil ATR spectra span 4000–2000 cm⁻¹ (2.5–5 µm), so mid-IR needs CIR or PIR fiber.

A remote analyzer in another building cannot be justified yet: the sources document 100–300 m reach only for low-OH Vis-NIR silica, and the mid-IR comparison of hollow waveguides and PIR fiber is shown only for 2 m lengths.
Approval is asked before the facts allow it: fiber type, link length, routing and operating conditions are not supplied, and method selection depends on them.
The published water-in-petroleum ATR example is a reason to test the method, not proof for this line: it gives no detection limit, fiber link length or process conditions.

methods.why: An application example exists for water in petroleum with an ATR probe, and ATR fiber probes analyse liquids at a distance from the spectrometer using high-transmission mid-IR fibers.
NIR runs on silica fiber and is the most common online fiber-probe method, but the sources give no NIR water-in-oil data.
Water absorbs Raman weakly, which suits aqueous media, but Raman needs special probes and the sources give no Raman data for water in oil.
Fluorescence needs an intrinsic fluorescent component, and most chemicals do not fluoresce; no fluorescence route for water is documented.

questions.q: What is the fiber link length, and how is the route laid between the petroleum line and the analyzer building?
questions.why: MIR reach is undocumented beyond short lengths, so the link length decides whether any mid-IR fiber is feasible.

questions.q: What water range, and what accuracy or detection limit, must the measurement meet?
questions.why: The example covers only 0.1–2.0% water and gives no detection limit, so the target sets the test design.

questions.q: What are the operating conditions (temperature, pressure, flow, oil type) at the probe point?
questions.why: The example slide gives no process conditions, and probe suitability depends on them.

questions.q: Can you supply oil samples with known water content, with reference values from independent laboratory analysis?
questions.why: Lab ATR tests come first, and reference values must come from independent laboratory analyses.

questions.q: What is the fiber type and specification of the existing silica cable?
questions.why: This confirms whether it is Vis-NIR silica (350–2400 nm), which cannot carry the mid-IR ATR range.

experiment.objective: Test whether water content in oil can be measured by MIR ATR, and whether the NIR silica option is a usable alternative, before any fiber link is approved.
steps: Prepare or obtain petroleum samples at several water contents spanning the target range, with water content set by independent laboratory analysis.
Record MIR ATR spectra over 4000–2000 cm⁻¹ with a ZrO2-tip ATR probe in a PEEK shaft, as in the example.
Check whether absorbance rises with water content, as in the example, and whether the signal separates the water levels.
Repeat the same samples on an NIR transmission or transflection probe with the silica cable for comparison.
Build a chemometric model on training samples and validate it on separate samples; do not derive accuracy from a few spectra.
references: AFS slide set, S02 p.13 (water in petroleum application)
AFS slide set, S02 p.6 (fiber transmission ranges)
experiment.go_no_go: Criteria come from the client; none are stated in the enquiry.

pathway.key_features: Absorbance rise with water content in the 4000–2000 cm⁻¹ range shown for the oil-water example.
pathway.path_reason: Lab tests and key-feature selection are needed first, and the fiber link length is unknown.

multispectral.combination: MIR ATR + NIR (only if MIR ATR alone fails on the same validation samples)
multispectral.why: MIR gives well-defined absorption peaks while NIR gives broad overlapping bands, so NIR may add complementary information, but no combined gain is documented for water in petroleum.
multispectral.test: Build MIR-only and MIR+NIR models on the same validation samples; the combination must beat MIR ATR alone to be adopted.

assumptions: Assumption: the oil type and water range are as in the example (0.1–2.0% water) until the client supplies them.
Assumption: the analyzer building is far enough away that a fiber link is needed; the length is unknown.
Assumption: the probe point on the line is accessible for an ATR probe; location not supplied.
